objective: By the end of this lesson you can link the symptoms of each aeromedical problem on the ACS list to its cause and its fix, apply the alcohol, drug and oxygen rules a paid pilot works under, and run an honest fitness and personal minimums check, using ADM, SRM and CRM tools when a client or a boss is pushing you to go.
why: About 80 percent of aviation accidents are tied to human factors, not to the airplane [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]], and pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than aircraft system failures [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]]. Once people pay you to fly, someone is waiting, a schedule is set and a paycheck is on the line, and external pressure is the one risk factor that can make a pilot ignore all the others [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

prereading.what: Hypoxia, hyperventilation, ears and sinuses, disorientation and illusions, motion sickness, carbon monoxide, stress, fatigue, dehydration, alcohol, drugs and scuba diving. The core of this lesson.
prereading.label: PHAK 17-3 to 17-19

prereading.what: Fitness for flight, effects of altitude, ear and sinus block, scuba waits, hyperventilation, carbon monoxide and illusions. Where the AIM and the PHAK give different numbers, use the AIM.
prereading.label: AIM 8-1-1 to 8-1-5

prereading.what: Risk management principles, hazard and risk, hazardous attitudes, the risk matrix, IMSAFE, PAVE and managing external pressure.
prereading.label: PHAK 2-3 to 2-10

prereading.what: SRM, the 5P check, the 3P model with PAVE, CARE and TEAM, DECIDE, operational pitfalls, situational awareness and workload.
prereading.label: PHAK 2-13 to 2-25

prereading.what: How to build baseline personal minimums and adjust them for fatigue, unfamiliar airplanes, unfamiliar airports and deadlines.
prereading.label: RMH 2-1 to 2-5

prereading.what: Threat and error management, expectation bias and confirmation bias, and the defenses a pilot builds.
prereading.label: RMH 6-1 to 6-5

prereading.what: The alcohol and drug rule word for word. Then read 91.211 (oxygen), 61.15 and 61.16 (alcohol and drug offenses) and 61.53 (medical deficiency).
prereading.label: 14 CFR 91.17

warmup: Think first: the regulations let you fly 8 hours after a beer, and they do not make you use oxygen until the cabin is above 12,500 ft. Yet the AIM tells you to wait 12 to 24 hours after drinking and to use oxygen above 10,000 ft by day. Why would the FAA write a rule and then recommend something stricter? Which one should you plan around when someone is paying you to fly?

key_terms.def: Not enough oxygen, most dangerous for the brain. Its four forms are hypoxic, hypemic, stagnant and histotoxic [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]].
The longest time you have to make and carry out rational, life-saving decisions at a given altitude without supplemental oxygen [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Breathing too fast and too deep, so the body loses too much carbon dioxide [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].
Not knowing the airplane's position, attitude or movement in space, usually when the eyes lose outside references [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].
A rapid acceleration, such as on takeoff, feels like a nose-up attitude, so the pilot may push into a dive [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].
Pressure trapped in the middle ear, usually on descent, that the pilot cannot equalize. It causes severe pain and hearing loss [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].
Nitrogen dissolved in the body comes out as bubbles when pressure drops; the most common symptom is joint pain, the bends [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Grams of alcohol per deciliter of blood or per 210 liters of breath. 0.04 or greater bars crew duty [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].
Managing every resource on board and outside the airplane, before and during flight, so a lone pilot gets a safe outcome [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].
In a two-pilot crew, the pilot who monitors the flightpath and energy, calls out deviations and intervenes if needed [[59:24|AC 120-71B 6.4]] [[59:25|AC 120-71B 6.4]].
Keeping a wrong picture of the situation even when evidence shows it is wrong [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].
Pushing aside information that does not fit what you expect, instead of letting it trigger an 'uh-oh' [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

chunks.title: Fit to fly when flying is your job

body.p: Exercising commercial pilot privileges in an airplane needs at least a second-class medical certificate [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23]]. Holding the certificate is not the same as being fit today. The AIM's safest rule is not to fly while suffering from any illness, and to call an Aviation Medical Examiner (AME) if that seems too strict for a particular illness [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

Even a minor illness can impair judgment, memory, alertness and the ability to calculate, and the medicine that controls the symptoms can itself lower performance [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]]. Pilot impairment contributes to many more accidents than aircraft system failures, which is why the FAA wants a preflight checklist on yourself as well as the airplane [[34:182|AIM 8-1-1]].

head: IMSAFE item
The question to ask yourself
rows: Have I taken prescription or over-the-counter drugs? [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]
Am I under pressure from work, money, health or family? [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]
Have I been drinking within 8 hours? Within 24 hours? [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]
Am I tired and not adequately rested? [[30:24|RMH 3-6]]

body.p: Some publications use the 'E' for Eating instead, because food and water intake matter on a long flight [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. Either way, the point is the same: the RMH treats the pilot as a hazard to be checked, just like the weather or the airplane [[30:23|RMH 3-5]].

callout.text: You are your own quality control. A fatigued pilot who has flown 16 hours, asked if he is too tired to continue, may answer 'no.' Goal-oriented pilots tend to deny their limits when asked to take a flight [[1:45|PHAK 2-6]].
Legal is the floor, not the target. Personal minimums are limits stricter than the regulations, set for 'smart' and 'safe' [[30:13|RMH 2-1]].

check.q: Which class of medical certificate do you need to exercise commercial privileges in an airplane, and does holding it make you fit to fly today?
check.a: At least second class [[60:204|14 CFR 61.23]]. No: you still check yourself every flight, because illness or medicine can impair you even with a valid certificate [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

body.p: Hypoxia means not enough oxygen. Any tissue suffers, but the brain is the big worry in flight, because any loss of mental function can lead to a fatal error [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]. The four types are named for their cause.

head: Type
What goes wrong
Flight examples
rows: Not enough oxygen reaches the lungs. At altitude the oxygen percentage is the same, but its partial pressure is lower [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]
Climbing without supplemental oxygen; CO2 from dry ice displacing cabin air [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]
The blood cannot carry enough oxygen [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]
Carbon monoxide (the most common cause), anemia, blood loss, a recent blood donation [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]
Oxygen-rich blood is not flowing to the tissues [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]
High G loads; cold that cuts circulation to hands and feet [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]
Cells cannot use the oxygen they get [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]
Alcohol, narcotics, poisons. One ounce of alcohol can equal about 2,000 ft more physiological altitude [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]

body.p: Symptoms include cyanosis (blue lips and fingernails), headache, slower reactions, impaired judgment, euphoria, visual impairment, drowsiness, dizziness, tingling and numbness. The early ones can be euphoria and a carefree feeling, and the worst part is the false sense that everything is fine [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

The AIM gives altitude bands for a healthy pilot. Night vision starts to suffer at a cabin altitude as low as 5,000 ft. Other big effects usually wait until 12,000 ft. From 12,000 to 15,000 ft, judgment, memory, alertness, coordination and math all degrade, and performance can seriously deteriorate within 15 minutes at 15,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Above 15,000 ft you get tunnel vision and cyanosis [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]].

callout.text: The PHAK table lists 30 minutes or more at 20,000 ft, but the AIM says the ability to take corrective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft and 20 to 30 minutes at 18,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Plan with the AIM numbers.

body.p: Things that lower your tolerance: CO from smoking or exhaust, anemia, some medicines, small amounts of alcohol, antihistamines, tranquilizers, sedatives and analgesics. Heat, cold, fever and anxiety raise the body's oxygen demand [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. Treatment is lower altitude, supplemental oxygen, or both [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]].

callout.text: Commercial cargo note: dry ice turns into large amounts of CO2 that can push oxygen out of a small cabin. Above 10 percent CO2 can cause convulsions, coma or death, and dry ice must never ride in a sealed container [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]].

check.q: A pilot gave blood three days ago. Which kind of hypoxia is she more exposed to, and why?
check.a: Hypemic hypoxia. Blood volume can take several weeks to return to normal after a donation, so the blood carries less oxygen [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]].

head: Source
What it says about oxygen
rows: Cabin above 12,500 ft up to 14,000 ft: required crew use oxygen for the part over 30 minutes. Above 14,000 ft: required crew use it the whole time. Above 15,000 ft: every occupant must be provided oxygen [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]
Each pilot uses oxygen above 10,000 ft through 12,000 ft for the part over 30 minutes, and continuously above 12,000 ft [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]]
Use oxygen above 10,000 ft by day and above 5,000 ft at night for best protection [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]

body.p: Notice the pattern. The Part 91 rule is a minimum. A charter operator under Part 135 must start oxygen 2,500 ft lower. The AIM recommendation is lower still. As a paid pilot, plan to the strictest one that applies to your flight.

Pressurized airplanes add training. To act as PIC of a pressurized airplane whose service ceiling or maximum operating altitude, whichever is lower, is above 25,000 ft, you need logged ground training covering respiration, hypoxia, time of useful consciousness, gas expansion, bubble formation and decompression, plus flight training in a pressurized airplane (or a simulator or FTD that represents one), each with an endorsement [[60:214|14 CFR 61.31(g)]].

Hyperventilation is the other breathing problem. A stressful moment can make you breathe too fast without noticing, which blows off carbon dioxide [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]]. Symptoms are lightheadedness, a feeling of suffocation, drowsiness, tingling and coolness, then incoordination, muscle spasms and finally unconsciousness [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

The fix is to bring the rate and depth of breathing back under control; symptoms usually fade within a few minutes. Breathing into a paper bag or talking aloud helps [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]] [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

callout.text: Early hypoxia and hyperventilation feel alike, and both can happen at once. If you are on oxygen when symptoms start, set the regulator to 100 percent and check that the system is working before you work on your breathing [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

check.q: You fly a Part 135 charter at 11,500 ft in an unpressurized single. When must you be on oxygen?
check.a: For the part of the flight at that altitude that lasts more than 30 minutes [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]]. Under Part 91 alone, no oxygen would be required at 11,500 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

chunks.title: Trapped gas and evolved gas: ears, sinuses, scuba

body.p: Gas in body cavities expands as you climb. On the way up, middle ear air usually escapes down the Eustachian tube by itself. On the way down you must open the tube yourself by swallowing, yawning or tensing your throat; if that fails, use the Valsalva maneuver: close the mouth, pinch the nose and gently try to blow through the nostrils [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

A cold, sore throat or nasal allergy can block the tube, causing an ear block: severe pain and hearing loss that can last hours to days, and even a ruptured eardrum [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. A sinus block happens the same way, most often in descent, with pain over the eyebrows or cheeks and sometimes aching upper teeth or bloody mucus [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Slow descent rates can reduce the pain [[1:427|PHAK 17-5]].

callout.text: Prevention is not flying with an upper respiratory infection or nasal allergy. Decongestant sprays usually do not protect you, and oral decongestants have side effects that can impair you. If a block does not clear soon after landing, see a physician [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

body.p: Scuba diving loads the body with extra nitrogen. Flying too soon lets it bubble out at low cabin pressure, which can create a serious in-flight emergency [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

head: Dive
Wait before flying up to 8,000 ft MSL
Wait before flying above 8,000 ft MSL

body.p: Table source: [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]] [[1:441|PHAK 17-19]]. The altitudes are actual flight altitudes above MSL, not cabin altitudes, because the cabin could lose pressure [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

callout.text: If DCS shows up in flight: oxygen at 100 percent, emergency descent, land as soon as possible and get medical help even if the symptoms go away. Keep a painful joint still [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

check.q: Your charter passenger made a dive with decompression stops this morning. How long should she wait before your 6,500 ft flight?
check.a: At least 24 hours, because the dive required a controlled ascent [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

chunks.title: Spatial disorientation: when the inner ear lies

body.p: Three systems tell you where you are: the vestibular system in the inner ear, the somatosensory system (skin, muscles and joints, the 'seat of the pants') and your eyes. In VMC the eyes usually win. Take away the horizon and the other two can fool you quickly [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

The semicircular canals sense rotation, but a slow roll of about 2 degrees per second or less goes unnoticed [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Your body also cannot tell gravity from the forces of maneuvering [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]].

head: Illusion
What causes it
The dangerous reaction
rows: Leveling after a slow, unnoticed bank [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Rolling back into the old bank or leaning toward it [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
An abrupt head movement in a long constant-rate turn [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Maneuvering into a dangerous attitude to stop a rotation that is not real [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Losing altitude in a turn that no longer feels like a turn [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Pulling back, which tightens the spiral [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Rapid acceleration on takeoff; or a quick power reduction [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Pushing nose-low; or pulling into a stall attitude [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Sloping clouds, ground light patterns, a lone light stared at in the dark [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Banking to match a false horizon; losing control chasing the light [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]

body.p: Defenses: train on instruments before flying in visibility under 3 miles or with no visible horizon, avoid sudden head movement during takeoffs, turns and approaches, and be rested and healthy, because illness, medication, alcohol, fatigue and mild hypoxia all raise your susceptibility. Most of all, trust the instruments [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]] [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]].

callout.text: The coriolis illusion is called the most overwhelming of all illusions in flight. Retrieve a dropped chart with minimal head movement [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

check.q: You lift off on a dark night over water and feel a strong pitch-up. What illusion is likely and what do you do?
check.a: The somatogravic illusion from the takeoff acceleration [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Do not push the nose down on feel; hold the takeoff attitude on the attitude indicator, because only instruments or fixed ground references prevent disorientation [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]].

body.p: Landing illusions make you misjudge your height above and distance from the threshold [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. The pattern to learn: anything that makes you feel high makes you fly low, and anything that makes you feel low makes you fly high.

head: Condition
Feels like
Error if not recognized
rows: Lower approach; may strike objects or land short [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Leveling out high, landing hard or overshooting [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]
Featureless terrain: water, dark areas, snow

body.p: Extremely clear air at a high airport can make you feel closer than you are, leading to a high approach and maybe a go-around [[1:432|PHAK 17-10]]. Lights along a road, or even a moving train, can be mistaken for runway or approach lights [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

bullets: Before an unfamiliar airport, read the airport diagram and Chart Supplement for slope, terrain and lighting [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Cross-check the altimeter often on every approach, day and night [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Fly over and look at an unfamiliar airport before landing when you can [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Use VASI, PAPI or an electronic glideslope whenever available [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
Expect approach accidents to rise when an emergency or other activity distracts you from usual procedures [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

check.q: You usually land on a 150 ft wide runway. Today's runway is 60 ft wide and slopes uphill. What will your eyes tell you, and what error follows?
check.a: Both illusions make you feel higher than you are, so you will tend to fly a lower approach [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. Use the PAPI or VASI and the altimeter [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

body.p: Motion sickness comes from the brain getting conflicting messages about the body's state. Signs are general discomfort, nausea, dizziness, paleness, sweating and vomiting. Anxiety and stress can feed it [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

bullets: Open the fresh air vents, look at objects outside the airplane and avoid unnecessary head movement [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].
Medicines like Dramamine can help passengers but are not recommended for the pilot, because they can cause drowsiness [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].
The PHAK's advice for students who get airsick is to avoid turbulent days and start with shorter flights [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Application: the same plan can help a nervous paying passenger.

body.p: Carbon monoxide (CO) is colorless, odorless and tasteless [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]]. It grabs hemoglobin about 200 times more easily than oxygen, causing hypemic hypoxia, and the body needs up to 48 hours to clear it [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Most light-airplane heaters warm air over the exhaust manifold, so a cracked manifold or leaking seal can feed CO into the cabin [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

Symptoms are headache, blurred vision, dizziness, drowsiness and loss of muscle power [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. CO can be present in dangerous amounts with no exhaust smell, so carry a CO detector [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

callout.text: Smell exhaust or feel these symptoms with the heater on: heater off, fresh air vents and windows open, supplemental oxygen if you have it. If symptoms are severe or continue after landing, get medical treatment [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

body.p: Smoking at sea level can raise blood CO enough to feel like 8,000 ft [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

check.q: Why is a CO detector worth carrying if you can always smell exhaust?
check.a: You cannot always smell it. CO can be present in dangerous amounts even when no exhaust odor is detected [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

chunks.title: Stress and fatigue on the job

body.p: Stress is the body's response to demands: adrenaline, higher heart rate, breathing and blood pressure [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. Some stress keeps you alert; performance rises with stress, peaks, then drops fast once stress passes your ability to cope [[1:60|PHAK 2-21]]. Acute stress is a short-term threat. Chronic stress is an ongoing load (money, work, relationships) that pushes performance down sharply; a pilot in that state should not exercise airman privileges and should see a physician [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

Work stress hurts in a subtle way: it can distract you enough to take risks such as pressing into worsening weather to stay on schedule. Stress plus fatigue is an extremely hazardous combination [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

head: Acute fatigue
Chronic fatigue
rows: Normal tiredness after strain, excitement or lost sleep [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]
Not enough recovery time between bouts of acute fatigue [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]
Performance keeps falling and judgment is impaired, so you take unwarranted risks [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]
Rest and sleep, exercise and proper nutrition [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]
A prolonged rest; often a physician [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]] [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]

body.p: Skill fatigue is a kind of acute fatigue with two signs: timing disruption, where each part of a task is slightly off, and a narrowed perceptual field, where you focus on the center and neglect the periphery [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Fatigue may not be noticed until serious errors are made [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

callout.text: Part 135 example: on unscheduled (on-demand) flights a one-pilot crew may not exceed 8 hours of flight time in any 24 consecutive hours, counting all commercial flying, unless the duty period exception in 135.267(c) applies [[6:93|14 CFR 135.267]].

Obstructive sleep apnea interrupts restorative sleep. Symptoms include snoring, daytime sleepiness and breathing pauses in sleep; get evaluated if you have them, a neck over 17 inches (men) or 16 inches (women), or a BMI over 30. Most treatments are acceptable for medical certification [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].
If you are suffering from acute fatigue, stay on the ground. No amount of training or experience overcomes fatigue in the flight deck [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

check.q: What two changes in your flying point to skill fatigue?
check.a: Timing disruption, where the parts of a task are slightly off, and disruption of the perceptual field, where you fixate on the center and neglect the periphery [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

body.p: Dehydration is a critical loss of body water. Hot flight decks and ramps, wind, humidity and diuretics (coffee, tea, alcohol, caffeinated soft drinks) cause it. Its signs are headache, fatigue, cramps, sleepiness and dizziness, and the first one you notice is usually fatigue [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

bullets: Drink two to four quarts of water every 24 hours as a guide [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
Thirst arrives late, at about a 1.5 quart deficit or 2 percent of body weight, and a sip turns it off too soon [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].
On long flights carry water and drink often: about one quart per hour in severe heat stress, one pint per hour in moderate heat [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Heatstroke is the body losing control of its temperature. It may show as dehydration, or only as a sudden collapse [[1:436|PHAK 17-14]].

body.p: Nutrition: eat regular balanced meals and bring snacks for you and your passengers [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]. Missed meals bring low blood sugar, with distraction, a breakdown in habit patterns and a shorter attention span [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]. A balanced diet and rest are also how acute fatigue is prevented [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

Cold: the sources used here give no hypothermia symptoms or treatment. What they do say is that cold reduces blood flow to the hands and feet (a form of stagnant hypoxia) [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], that extreme cold raises the body's oxygen demand [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]], and that a trip over remote areas calls for clothing, water and survival gear in case of a forced landing [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].

callout.text: Application: on a winter charter, dress for the walk away from a forced landing, not for the heated cabin. Ask your CFI or another medical source for hypothermia signs and first aid.

check.q: On a 4-hour summer flight in moderate heat, how much water does the PHAK guide suggest?
check.a: About one pint per hour, so about 4 pints (2 quarts) [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

chunks.title: The rules: alcohol, drugs and medical deficiency

body.p: 14 CFR 91.17(a) says no person may act or attempt to act as a crewmember of a civil aircraft in any of these four cases [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]:

bullets: Within 8 hours after drinking any alcoholic beverage.
While under the influence of alcohol.
While using any drug that affects your faculties in any way contrary to safety.
While having an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater in a blood or breath specimen.

body.p: Each one stands alone. Nine hours after drinking but still at 0.05 is illegal. Ten hours and only 0.01 can still be illegal if you are under the influence [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

head: Rule
What it requires
rows: Except in an emergency, no pilot may carry a person who appears intoxicated or under the influence of drugs, unless a medical patient under proper care [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]
Submit to a law enforcement officer's alcohol test when authorized; give the FAA test results taken within 4 hours of acting as crewmember when it has a reasonable basis [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]
Breaking 91.17(a) is grounds for denial of an application for up to 1 year, or suspension or revocation [[60:201|14 CFR 61.15]] [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15]]

Two motor vehicle actions (such as a DUI conviction or license suspension) from separate incidents within 3 years are grounds for action, and you must report each one in writing to the FAA within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15]]
Refusing the alcohol test, or refusing to release results, is grounds for denial, suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.16]]

No PIC or required crewmember duty while you know or have reason to know of a medical condition, or take medication or treatment, that would make you fail your required medical [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]]

body.p: Drug convictions also count. A conviction under any Federal or State drug law is grounds for denial of an application for up to 1 year after the final conviction, or suspension or revocation [[60:201|14 CFR 61.15]]. The FAA states that marijuana is an illicit drug under federal law and its use by airmen is prohibited [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

callout.text: In the CFRs, crewmember duty while using any medication that affects your faculties contrary to safety is prohibited. The AIM's safest rule is to fly as a crewmember while taking no medication unless the FAA approves it [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

check.q: Your last drink was 10 hours ago, but a breath test would read 0.05. Can you fly?
check.a: No. The 8-hour rule is met, but an alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater is a separate prohibition [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

chunks.title: What alcohol, drugs and OTC medicine do to you

body.p: Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant that acts much like a general anesthetic. Even small amounts impair judgment, coordination, vision, memory and attention [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]]. As little as one ounce of liquor, one beer or four ounces of wine can impair flying skills, and it stays detectable for at least 3 hours [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

bullets: The body needs about 3 hours to clear one mixed drink or one beer, and large amounts can stay for over 16 hours [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
A hangover is still impairment. Nothing speeds up the destruction of alcohol [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]] [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Altitude multiplies alcohol: two drinks at altitude can act like three or four [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].
Alcohol can cause inner-ear disturbance and spatial disorientation for up to 48 hours [[1:439|PHAK 17-17]].

callout.text: The AIM's excellent rule: allow at least 12 to 24 hours from 'bottle to throttle,' depending on how much you drank [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]. The regulation's 8 hours is only the minimum [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

body.p: Medicines: tranquilizers, sedatives, strong pain relievers and cough suppressants impair judgment, memory, alertness, coordination, vision and math directly. Antihistamines, blood pressure drugs, muscle relaxants and anti-diarrhea and motion sickness agents can do the same as side effects. Any nervous system depressant makes you more prone to hypoxia [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]].

bullets: Diphenhydramine (for example Benadryl) causes drowsiness and has a long half-life, so the side effects last [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

Common OTC pain relievers (aspirin, acetaminophen, ibuprofen) usually do not restrict flying at the correct dose; prescription analgesics such as codeine or oxycodone almost always do [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].
After the first dose of any new medicine, wait at least 48 hours to see if you have side effects [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
After a medicine with possible sedating or dizzying side effects, wait at least five maximal dosing intervals: a 5 to 6 hour interval means 30 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Never mix drugs with alcohol, and do not take more than one drug at a time unless a physician prescribes it [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

callout.text: The illness you are treating may itself be disqualifying, even if the medicine is fine [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]]. When in doubt, ask an AME before you fly [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

check.q: A cold medicine with a 12-hour dosing interval makes you drowsy. How long after the last dose should you wait to fly?
check.a: At least five maximal dosing intervals: 5 x 12 = 60 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

chunks.title: ADM, SRM and CRM for the paid pilot

body.p: Aeronautical decision-making (ADM) is a systematic way to find the best course of action for a given set of circumstances [[1:40|PHAK 2-1]]. Risk management is part of it, and it rests on four principles: accept no unnecessary risk, make risk decisions at the right level (you are PIC, so never let ATC or passengers make them for you), accept risk only when benefits outweigh costs, and build risk management into every stage of the flight [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

The matrix scores a hazard by likelihood (probable, occasional, remote, improbable) and severity (catastrophic, critical, marginal, negligible). A non-instrument-rated pilot facing an occasional chance of IMC lands in the high-risk box: do not fly, or fly only after mitigating, eliminating or controlling the risk [[1:45|PHAK 2-6]]. A scored form like Figure 2-6 adds sleep, health, weather, time of day and planning into one number [[1:46|PHAK 2-7]].

head: Tool
How to use it
rows: Perceive hazards (Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures); Process them (Consequences, Alternatives, Reality, External factors); Perform (Transfer, Eliminate, Accept, Mitigate) [[1:54|PHAK 2-15]]

Review the Plan, Plane, Pilot, Passengers and Programming at preflight, before takeoff, at midpoint (hourly if over 2 hours), before descent and before the final approach fix or pattern entry [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]] [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]]
Detect, Estimate, Choose, Identify, Do, Evaluate: a loop for problems that develop in flight [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]]
In emergencies, experts take the first workable option they recognize; that skill grows from training and experience [[1:60|PHAK 2-21]]

body.p: SRM is managing all resources, on board and outside, so a single pilot gets a safe outcome. It covers ADM, risk management, task and automation management, CFIT awareness and situational awareness [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]]. Your resources include the passenger in the right seat (traffic watch, reading checklist items), ATC and flight service [[1:62|PHAK 2-23]].

CRM is the crew version: the effective use of all resources, people, hardware and information, to make good decisions [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]]. In a two-pilot operation one pilot is the pilot flying (PF) and one the pilot monitoring (PM). The PF manages the flightpath and energy; the PM monitors them, calls out deviations and intervenes if needed; control changes hands with a verbal handoff and a verbal acceptance [[59:24|AC 120-71B 6.4]] [[59:25|AC 120-71B 6.4]].

Workload is not even. Takeoff and initial climb are about 2 percent of flight time but 23.4 percent of accidents, and landing alone is 24.1 percent [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]]. Plan, prioritize and sequence tasks: set radios and brief charts early, and finish checklists before high-workload phases [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

check.q: In the TEAM step, hiring a CFI to ride along on a challenging trip is which choice?
check.a: Mitigate: the risk is reduced by flying with another pilot, not removed or handed off [[1:57|PHAK 2-18]].

head: Hazardous attitude
Sounds like
Antidote
rows: Follow the rules. They are usually right [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]
'Do it quickly.' The first idea wins [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]
'I can do it.' Taking risks to impress [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]
'What's the use?' Going along with unreasonable requests to be a nice guy [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]
I'm not helpless. I can make a difference [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]

body.p: Recognize the thought, label it as hazardous, then say the antidote [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. Paid flying adds external pressure: someone waiting, a passenger you do not want to disappoint, the urge to prove yourself, 'get-there-itis,' and pride. External pressure is the one factor that can make you ignore all the other risks, and it figures into a majority of accidents [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]] [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

bullets: Build in time for an extra fuel or weather stop, and have backup plans for must-arrive trips [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
Manage passengers' and the boss's expectations; the PHAK's example pilot with 4 hours of sleep turned down a 750-mile trip and later convinced the unhappy boss [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].
If you hear yourself say it will 'probably' be okay, do a solid reality check [[1:55|PHAK 2-16]].

body.p: Distraction and lost situational awareness: fatigue, stress and work overload make pilots fixate on one item. Many accidents start with a minor problem, such as a gauge reading wrong, that pulls attention away from flying the airplane [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. The first sign of overload is working harder but getting less done; then attention narrows to one item. The fix is to stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

callout.text: Part 135 sterile flight deck: during critical phases (taxi, takeoff, landing and all flight below 10,000 ft except cruise) crewmembers may do only duties needed for safe operation, and no distracting activity is allowed [[6:33|14 CFR 135.100]].

body.p: Expectation bias is holding on to a wrong picture despite evidence, as when a pilot read a changed runway closure NOTAM but still saw it the old way and began an approach to the closed runway. Confirmation bias is suppressing information that does not fit the expectation. Either way you keep flying a plan the facts no longer support, and fatigue makes both more likely [[30:45|RMH 6-2]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

Threat and error management thinks in layers. Threats come from outside (weather, failures, ATC changes); errors are your own deviations. Defenses such as checklists, SOPs, a second pilot, clear briefings and proficiency are the slices of cheese; the more proficient and disciplined you are, the less likely the holes line up [[30:44|RMH 6-1]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]] [[30:47|RMH 6-4]] [[30:48|RMH 6-5]].

check.q: How does confirmation bias differ from expectation bias, and what do they share?
check.a: Expectation bias is a wrong assessment that persists despite evidence; confirmation bias is pushing aside information that does not fit the expectation. Both leave you continuing a plan despite clues that the situation is not what you think [[30:45|RMH 6-2]] [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

chunks.title: Checkride skills: self-assessment and common errors

body.p: For S1 the examiner picks at least three conditions from the K1 list and you link symptoms and effects to causes and corrective actions (ACS CA.I.H.S1). For S2 you assess yourself, including fitness for flight and personal minimums, for the real flight or a scenario the examiner gives (ACS CA.I.H.S2).

Then adjust for today. For each special condition, such as illness, medication, stress or fatigue; an unfamiliar airplane or avionics; an unfamiliar airport; or a 'must meet' deadline, add at least 500 ft to the ceiling, 1/2 mile to visibility and 500 ft to runway length, and subtract at least 5 knots from winds [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Never lower your minimums to make a specific flight; adjust them only when you are not under pressure [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

head: Common error
Fix
rows: Treating 'legal' as 'fit': 8 hours and 0.04 met, so go
Use the AIM's 12 to 24 hours and IMSAFE [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]]
Diagnosing hyperventilation and slowing breathing while on oxygen without checking the system
100 percent oxygen and a system check first [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]]
48 hours after a new medicine; five dosing intervals for sedating ones [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]]
Using cabin altitude for scuba waits
The waits use actual flight altitude MSL [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]]
Trusting feel in a dark takeoff or a long turn
Adjusting personal minimums on the ramp under pressure
Set them in advance and stick to the plan [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]

callout.text: Bring a written personal minimums sheet to the checkride. A written set also makes it easier to explain a no-go to passengers who depend on your judgment [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

check.q: Your baseline day minimums are 2,500 ft and 4 miles. You are tired after a long workday and flying an airplane with unfamiliar avionics. What are today's minimums at least?
check.a: Two conditions: add 2 x 500 ft and 2 x 1/2 mile. 2,500 + 1,000 = 3,500 ft and 4 + 1 = 5 miles [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

f1.caption: Figure 17-1. Time of useful consciousness. (PHAK 17-4)
f1.alt: A two-column table of altitude and time of useful consciousness: 45,000 ft 9 to 15 seconds; 40,000 ft 15 to 20 seconds; 35,000 ft 30 to 60 seconds; 30,000 ft 1 to 2 minutes; 28,000 ft 2 and a half to 3 minutes; 25,000 ft 3 to 5 minutes; 22,000 ft 5 to 10 minutes; 20,000 ft 30 minutes or more.

f2.caption: Figure 17-3. The semicircular canals lie in three planes and sense motions of roll, pitch, and yaw. (PHAK 17-6)
f2.alt: Left: an airplane with curved arrows for roll, pitch and yaw, and a note that the semicircular tubes sit at about right angles to each other. Middle: a cutaway of the inner ear. Right: an enlarged canal base labeled ampulla, semicircular canals, otolith organ, endolymph fluid, cupola, hair cells and vestibular nerve.

f3.caption: Figure 17-6. Sensations from centrifugal force. (PHAK 17-8)
f3.alt: Six front views of an airplane with a seated pilot and a red arrow for the force the pilot feels. Level, coordinated turn and pull out all push the pilot straight down into the seat. Level skid, forward slip and uncoordinated turn push the pilot sideways. The note says skid, slip and uncoordinated turns feel similar.

f4.caption: Figure 17-7. Runway illusions. (PHAK 17-11)
f4.alt: Paired scenes. A narrower runway makes the pilot fly a lower approach than the dotted normal path; a wider runway makes the pilot fly higher. A downsloping runway leads to a higher approach and an upsloping runway to a lower approach. Text boxes explain each illusion.

f5.caption: Figure 2-1. The percentage of aviation accidents as they relate to the different phases of flight. Phase names are cropped off for the labeling game. (PHAK 2-2)
f5.alt: Nine red bars along a flight path from taxi to landing, with values 3.5, 23.4, 3.3, 15.7, 2.6, 13, 9.7, 24.1 and 4.7 percent. Bands above show takeoff and initial climb is 2 percent of flight time, the middle phases 83 percent and the last phases 15 percent.

f6.caption: Figure 2-5. This risk matrix can be used for almost any operation by assigning likelihood and consequence. (PHAK 2-6)
f6.alt: A grid with likelihood down the side (probable, occasional, remote, improbable) and severity across the top (catastrophic, critical, marginal, negligible). Probable with catastrophic or critical, and occasional with catastrophic, are High. Other cells are Serious, Medium or Low.

f7.caption: Figure 6-1. The Swiss cheese model. (RMH 6-5)
f7.alt: Threat arrows pass through three stacks of cheese slices labeled Prevent, Trap and Mitigate, with Errors and Undesired aircraft state between them, ending at an Incident/Accident burst. Above are the words Anticipate, Recognize and Recover.

scenario.title: The aerial photo job with a deadline
scenario.setup: You are a new commercial pilot hired for a Part 91 aerial photography job in an unpressurized single with portable oxygen. The photographer wants 45 minutes of shots from 13,500 ft MSL over a coastal city at 1400 today, then lower shots of the shoreline, returning at dusk over water and haze to a runway that slopes uphill. He finished a no-decompression scuba dive at 0900 this morning. You slept 5 hours. His magazine deadline is tomorrow, and he tells you other pilots would just go. Your written baseline day minimums are 3,000 ft and 5 miles; the forecast is 3,500 ft and 6 miles.

questions.q: Use PAVE to name the main hazards before you even look at the airplane.
questions.a: Pilot: 5 hours of sleep, a fatigue hazard [[30:23|RMH 3-5]]. Aircraft: unpressurized, oxygen needed. Environment: dusk over water, haze, sloping runway. External pressures: the deadline and the 'other pilots would go' comment [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]] [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]].

questions.q: Can the photographer fly to 13,500 ft at 1400 today?
questions.a: No. Above 8,000 ft MSL the wait is at least 24 hours after any dive, so not before 0900 tomorrow. Even below 8,000 ft he should wait 12 hours, until 2100 [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

questions.q: If the high shots move to tomorrow, what does 91.211 require for 45 minutes at 13,500 ft, and what would you do?
questions.a: Between 12,500 and 14,000 ft the required crew must use oxygen for the part over 30 minutes: 45 - 30 = 15 minutes. Passengers need not be provided oxygen below 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]]. The AIM recommends oxygen above 10,000 ft by day, so plan to use it from 10,000 ft and offer it to the photographer [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

questions.q: Apply your personal minimums to today's forecast.
questions.a: Two special conditions, fatigue and a 'must meet' deadline, each add at least 500 ft and 1/2 mile: 3,000 + 1,000 = 4,000 ft and 5 + 1 = 6 miles [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. A 3,500 ft forecast is below that, so today is a no-go for this flight.

questions.q: The photographer says other pilots would go. What attitude is he baiting, and how do you answer?
questions.a: Macho: proving yourself by taking risks. The antidote is 'Taking chances is foolish' [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]]. Manage his expectations and offer a plan with a backup, such as tomorrow morning after rest [[1:49|PHAK 2-10]].

questions.q: On a later dusk return over water with haze to the uphill runway, which illusions should you expect and how do you guard against them?
questions.a: Shoreline lights can create a false horizon [[1:448|PHAK 17-26]]. Haze, featureless water and an upsloping runway all tend to make you fly a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. Fly the instruments, check the altimeter often and use the PAPI or VASI [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].

skills.do: For at least three conditions from K1a to K1l that the examiner chooses, tie the symptoms and effects to the causes and the corrective actions (ACS CA.I.H.S1). There is no numeric tolerance; the examiner listens for correct, complete links.
skills.practice: Make a card for all twelve conditions with symptoms, cause and fix, and quiz yourself in random order. Start with hypoxia versus hyperventilation and CO, since their symptoms overlap [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]] [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

skills.do: Assess your own fitness and personal minimums for the actual flight or the examiner's scenario (ACS CA.I.H.S2): run IMSAFE, compare the weather and runway to your written minimums, adjust them for the day's conditions and make a go, no-go or mitigate decision.
skills.practice: Fill out the RMH baseline personal minimums tables, then practice adjusting them for made-up days with fatigue, a new airplane or a deadline [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] [[30:17|RMH 2-5]]. Score real flights on a form like PHAK Figure 2-6 [[1:46|PHAK 2-7]].

quiz.q: According to the AIM, how long do you have to take corrective action at a cabin altitude of 20,000 ft without oxygen?
options: 5 to 12 minutes
20 to 30 minutes
30 minutes or more
9 to 15 seconds
quiz.why: The AIM says corrective and protective ability is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at 20,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. 30 minutes or more is the older PHAK table value [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], and 20 to 30 minutes is the AIM's number for 18,000 ft.

quiz.q: You cruise an unpressurized airplane under Part 91 at 14,500 ft MSL for 20 minutes. What does 91.211 require?
options: Every occupant must use oxygen
Nothing, because the time is under 30 minutes
The required crew must use oxygen the whole time above 14,000 ft
Oxygen is only recommended
quiz.why: Above 14,000 ft the required minimum flight crew must use oxygen the entire time; the 30-minute allowance applies only from 12,500 to 14,000 ft, and every occupant must be provided oxygen only above 15,000 ft [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

quiz.q: Why does the AIM say to check your oxygen system before working on your breathing rate?
options: Hyperventilation only happens without oxygen
Slow breathing makes hypoxia worse
The regulator cannot be set to 100 percent
Early hypoxia and hyperventilation symptoms are alike, and both can happen at once
quiz.why: Early symptoms are similar and both can occur together, so set 100 percent oxygen and check the system first [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

quiz.q: When does a sinus block most often happen?
options: During descent
In level cruise
During the climb
On the ground before engine start
quiz.why: A sinus block occurs most frequently during descent [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].

quiz.q: In a long constant-rate turn in IMC, which action is most likely to trigger the coriolis illusion?
options: Holding the turn with small aileron inputs
Bending down to pick up a dropped chart
Scanning the attitude indicator
Reducing power slowly
quiz.why: An abrupt head movement in a prolonged constant-rate turn causes the coriolis illusion; retrieve dropped items with minimal head movement [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]] [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

quiz.q: Rain on the windscreen during an approach tends to make you:
options: Steepen the approach abruptly
Fly a higher approach
Fly a lower approach
Land long and fast
quiz.why: Rain on the windscreen creates an illusion of greater height, so the pilot flies a lower approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]].

quiz.q: How long can the body need to get rid of carbon monoxide?
options: About 3 hours
Up to 8 hours
Up to 24 hours
Up to 48 hours
quiz.why: The body requires up to 48 hours to dispose of CO [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

quiz.q: Which fatigue is not relieved by diet, rest and sleep, and usually needs a physician?
options: Acute fatigue
Skill fatigue
Flight fatigue after one long leg
Chronic fatigue
quiz.why: Chronic fatigue is not relieved by proper diet and rest and usually requires treatment by a physician [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

quiz.q: A commercial pilot with a second-class medical learns she has a condition that would fail the second-class standards. What does 61.53 say?
options: She may fly until the medical expires
She may fly only with a safety pilot
She may not act as PIC or a required pilot crewmember
She must report it within 60 days but may keep flying
quiz.why: No PIC or required crewmember duty while knowing or having reason to know of a condition that would make the pilot unable to meet the required medical [[60:233|14 CFR 61.53]].

quiz.q: Which statement about SRM is correct?
options: It means managing all resources on board and outside to get a safe outcome
It applies only to pilots with no autopilot
It replaces the need for checklists
It is used only in emergencies
quiz.why: SRM is managing all resources on board and from outside, before and during flight, so a single pilot gets a safe outcome [[1:43|PHAK 2-4]].

final_quiz.q: You carry a box of dry ice in the small cabin of a cargo flight. You notice you are breathing fast and your heart is racing. What is the most likely cause and the best action?
options: Hyperventilation from stress; breathe into a bag
Dehydration; drink water and continue
Carbon monoxide from the heater; turn up the heat
CO2 from the dry ice displacing oxygen; ventilate the cabin and land
final_quiz.why: Dry ice turns into CO2 that can push out oxygen; high CO2 brings faster breathing and a racing heart, and above 10 percent can cause convulsions or death [[1:425|PHAK 17-3]]. Application: treat the cause by getting fresh air into the cabin and landing.

final_quiz.q: Your last drink was at 0030. At 0900 a breath test would read 0.02, and you show no signs of being under the influence. Which is true?
options: Flying at 0900 meets 91.17, but the AIM advises 12 to 24 hours
Flying at 0900 is illegal because any alcohol is prohibited
You must wait until 0.00 under 91.17
You may fly once 6 hours have passed
final_quiz.why: 0030 to 0900 is 8.5 hours, more than 8, and 0.02 is below 0.04, so 91.17(a)(1) and (a)(4) are met as long as you are not under the influence [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]]. The AIM still recommends at least 12 to 24 hours between bottle and throttle [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

final_quiz.q: Your driver's license is suspended after a DUI arrest. What must you do as a certificated pilot?
options: Nothing until a conviction
Tell your AME at your next medical
Send a written report to the FAA within 60 days
Surrender your pilot certificate
final_quiz.why: A license suspension for impaired driving is a motor vehicle action, and each must be reported in writing to the FAA within 60 days [[60:202|14 CFR 61.15]].

final_quiz.q: An antihistamine caused you no trouble on the ground. Why could it hurt you at 9,500 ft?
options: Depressant drugs make the brain more susceptible to hypoxia
It thickens the blood
It blocks the Eustachian tubes
It raises carbon monoxide in the blood
final_quiz.why: Any medicine that depresses the nervous system, such as an antihistamine, can make a pilot more susceptible to hypoxia, and drugs with no ground effects can cause problems at fairly low altitudes [[34:180|AIM 8-1-1]] [[1:438|PHAK 17-16]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing out over a dark lake at night, you level off abruptly and feel as if you are tumbling backward. What is the risk?
options: Pulling up into a stall
Rolling into a steep bank
Pushing abruptly nose-low, which can deepen the illusion
Staring at a single light
final_quiz.why: That is the inversion illusion: the pilot may push abruptly nose-low, possibly making it worse [[34:185|AIM 8-1-5]]. Trust the attitude indicator.

final_quiz.q: Your baseline day minimums are 2,500 ft and 4 miles. You are flying to an unfamiliar airport with a client who must make a meeting. Using the RMH examples, what are your minimums today at least?
options: 2,500 ft and 4 miles
3,000 ft and 4 1/2 miles
4,000 ft and 6 miles
3,500 ft and 5 miles
final_quiz.why: Two conditions (unfamiliar airport, must-meet deadline), each adding at least 500 ft and 1/2 mile: 2,500 + 1,000 = 3,500 ft and 4 + 1 = 5 miles [[30:17|RMH 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: Your oil temperature creeps up. Sure the freshly overhauled engine is fine, you explain away the gauge, then push aside the rising cylinder temperature too, because neither fits your belief. The RMH names two biases and warns not to confuse them. Which one is its name for suppressing information that does not fit your expectation?
options: Expectation bias
Confirmation bias
Resignation
Skill fatigue
final_quiz.why: Suppressing information that does not fit your expectation, instead of triggering an internal 'uh-oh,' is confirmation bias, which the RMH says is not to be confused with expectation bias (a wrong assessment that persists despite evidence) [[30:45|RMH 6-2]].

final_quiz.q: In a two-pilot crew, the PM calls '1 dot high' twice and the PF does not respond or correct. In the AC 120-71B example, what does the PM do?
options: Wait for the PF to notice
If safety calls for it, say 'I have control, going around' and fly the go-around
Call it a third time, then log it
Ask ATC for a lower altitude
final_quiz.why: If the PF does not respond to two successive challenges, per the operator's SOP and if safety indicates, the PM calls 'I have control, going around' and initiates a go-around as PF [[59:26|AC 120-71B 6.6.2.3]].

final_quiz.q: On a Part 135 charter you descend through 8,000 ft toward the airport. A passenger asks you to point out sights. What applies?
options: Fine, because you are not in cruise
Allowed only by the copilot
Not allowed: below 10,000 ft except cruise is a critical phase where only safety duties are allowed
Allowed after the landing checklist
final_quiz.why: Critical phases include taxi, takeoff, landing and all flight below 10,000 ft except cruise; pointing out sights is named as a non-safety duty [[6:33|14 CFR 135.100]].

final_quiz.q: Your flight will last 3 1/2 hours. When should the en route 5P checks happen?
options: Only at the midpoint
Hourly, since the flight is over 2 hours
Only before descent
Every 15 minutes
final_quiz.why: The 5P check runs at preflight, before takeoff, at the midpoint, before descent and before the FAF or pattern; if the flight is longer than 2 hours it should be done hourly [[1:52|PHAK 2-13]] [[1:53|PHAK 2-14]].

final_quiz.q: A passenger insists on flying lower over his house. The pilot thinks, 'It's his charter, nothing I say matters,' and goes along. Which attitude and antidote fit?
options: Resignation: I'm not helpless, I can make a difference
Macho: taking chances is foolish
Impulsivity: not so fast, think first
Anti-authority: follow the rules
final_quiz.why: Resignation pilots leave action to others and go along with unreasonable requests to be a nice guy; the antidote is 'I'm not helpless. I can make a difference' [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]].

final_quiz.q: During a busy approach you notice you are working harder but getting less done. According to the PHAK, this is:
options: A sign of good workload management
The first effect of high workload, so stop, think, slow down and prioritize
Automation complacency, so hand-fly
Chronic fatigue, so land at once
final_quiz.why: The first effect of high workload is working harder but accomplishing less; the fix is to stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

final_quiz.q: A passenger made a no-decompression dive 14 hours ago. You will fly a pressurized airplane at FL230 with a cabin altitude of 7,000 ft. What does the AIM recommend?
options: Go: the cabin is below 8,000 ft and 12 hours have passed
Wait until 24 hours after the dive
Go if the passenger uses oxygen
Wait 48 hours
final_quiz.why: The scuba wait altitudes are actual flight altitudes MSL, not cabin altitudes. FL230 is above 8,000 ft, so wait at least 24 hours after any dive [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

takeaways: Legal is the floor: 8 hours and under 0.04 under 91.17, but the AIM says 12 to 24 hours.
Hypoxia comes in four types; know the AIM altitude bands and oxygen rules, and plan to the strictest one that applies.
If on oxygen and feeling odd: 100 percent and check the system before slowing your breathing.
Feel high, fly low: narrow or upsloping runways, featureless terrain, rain and haze. Use the PAPI and altimeter.
Heater on plus headache or drowsiness means CO: heater off, fresh air, oxygen, land.
Run IMSAFE and written personal minimums every flight, and adjust them before you are under pressure.
External pressure is the risk that hides all the others; name the hazardous attitude and say the antidote.
cfi_notes: Sources disagree at 20,000 ft: PHAK Figure 17-1 lists a time of useful consciousness of 30 minutes or more at 20,000 ft MSL [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], while the AIM says the ability to take corrective and protective action is lost in 5 to 12 minutes at a cabin pressure altitude of 20,000 ft [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]. This lesson teaches the AIM number; use the PHAK table for the altitudes above 20,000 ft.

Night vision: PHAK says it declines measurably above 4,000 ft pressure altitude [[1:446|PHAK 17-24]]; the AIM says deterioration occurs at a cabin altitude as low as 5,000 ft and recommends oxygen above 5,000 ft at night [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]] [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Teach the AIM values; the point is that night vision suffers low.
The PHAK gives two figures for accidents tied to human factors: about 80 percent [[1:41|PHAK 2-2]] and more than 70 percent [[1:50|PHAK 2-11]]. Do not test a single number.
The anti-authority antidote reads 'They are usually right' in the PHAK [[1:44|PHAK 2-5]] and 'They help prevent accidents' in the RMH [[30:21|RMH 3-3]]. Accept either wording.

PHAK says hypoxia symptoms vary with the individual [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; the AIM says they do not vary in an individual [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]]. Both support altitude chamber training: each pilot has a personal pattern worth learning.

Commercial students often quote only 91.211. Show them that a Part 135 job starts required oxygen above 10,000 ft [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]] and that the AIM recommends it there by day anyway [[34:183|AIM 8-1-2]].
S1 is the examiner's choice of three conditions, so the student must know all twelve. Hypothermia is on the list but these FAA sources do not describe it; supply it from another medical source.
Demonstrate disorientation only with an instructor or safety pilot at a safe altitude [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]. Even no sensation at all proves the point: the body cannot detect the bank.
For S2, have the student bring a filled-in RMH personal minimums sheet [[30:16|RMH 2-4]] and practice saying a no-go out loud to a 'client' played by the CFI.
gaps: K1j Hypothermia: a search of every loaded source (PHAK, AIM, RMH, AFH, IFH, AWH, the ACs and 14 CFR) finds no hypothermia symptoms, causes or treatment. Only related lines exist (cold reduces circulation [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]]; cold raises oxygen demand [[34:182|AIM 8-1-2]]; carry survival clothing over remote areas [[1:48|PHAK 2-9]]). A CFI or medical reference must fill this in.

K1i Nutrition: guidance is brief (balanced meals, snacks, low blood sugar effects, vitamin A for night vision) [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]] [[1:447|PHAK 17-25]]. No source gives specific meal timing or amounts.

Flight and rest limits: the rules read give limits for Part 135 [[6:93|14 CFR 135.267]] and for Part 91 subpart K fractional programs [[60:593|14 CFR 91.1059]], but none for other Part 91 commercial work such as aerial photography. Use employer policy and personal limits.
Specific medicines: the sources give categories and waiting rules, not a list of FAA-acceptable drugs. An AME must answer questions about any particular medication [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].
Operator drug and alcohol testing programs under Part 120 are only mentioned in passing in the rules read here; a Part 135 employer's program and training cover them.

activities.title: True or false: the alcohol and drug rules
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: An alcohol concentration of exactly 0.04 is legal for crew duty.
cards.why: False. 0.04 or greater is prohibited [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

cards.s: Even 10 hours after your last drink, you may not fly while under the influence of alcohol.
cards.why: True. Being under the influence is its own prohibition, separate from the 8-hour rule [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

cards.s: You may carry a passenger who appears intoxicated if he is a medical patient under proper care.
cards.why: True. That and an emergency are the only exceptions [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

cards.s: Refusing a lawful police alcohol test has no effect on your pilot certificate.
cards.why: False. Refusal is grounds for denial, suspension or revocation [[60:202|14 CFR 61.16]].

cards.s: Two motor vehicle actions within 3 years, from separate incidents, are grounds for suspension or revocation.
Because the regulations do not list stress as grounding, a stressed pilot is fit to fly.
cards.why: False. Stress is not on the grounding list, but the pilot should consider its effects on performance [[1:47|PHAK 2-8]]; chronic stress means do not exercise privileges [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]].

activities.title: Work the human factors numbers
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Part 91, unpressurized. You spend 75 minutes at a cabin altitude of 13,000 ft. For how many of those minutes must the required crew use oxygen?
items.why: Between 12,500 and 14,000 ft, oxygen is required for the part over 30 minutes: 75 - 30 = 45 minutes [[60:491|14 CFR 91.211]].

items.q: A passenger finished a no-decompression dive at 0930. You will cruise at 9,500 ft MSL. How many hours should she wait after the dive?
items.why: Above 8,000 ft MSL the wait is at least 24 hours after any dive; the 12-hour wait applies only up to 8,000 ft [[34:184|AIM 8-1-2]].

items.q: An allergy pill is taken every 8 hours and can cause drowsiness. Using the PHAK rule, how many hours after the last dose should you wait to fly?
items.why: Five maximal dosing intervals: 5 x 8 = 40 hours [[1:440|PHAK 17-18]].

items.q: A 4-hour flight in moderate heat stress. Using the PHAK guide of one pint per hour, how many quarts of water should you plan?
items.why: 4 hours x 1 pint = 4 pints; 2 pints = 1 quart, so 4 / 2 = 2 quarts [[1:437|PHAK 17-15]].

items.q: Score the PHAK Figure 2-6 form: slept under 8 hours, feel a bit off, destination weather 3 to 5 miles and 1,000 to 3,000 ft, 'one thing after another' day, night flight, rushed, did not use a computer program for all planning, verified W&B, evaluated performance, did not brief passengers. Total score?

Part 135 unscheduled (on-demand), one-pilot crew. You already flew 3.2 hours of commercial flying in the last 24 hours. Without the 135.267(c) exception, how many more hours may you fly in that 24-hour period?
items.why: Limit 8 hours in 24 consecutive hours for one pilot, counting all commercial flying: 8 - 3.2 = 4.8 hours [[6:93|14 CFR 135.267]].

activities.title: The early charter, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You fly a turbocharged, unpressurized single for a Part 135 on-demand operator. Tomorrow's trip: two passengers, 0600 departure, cruise at 11,500 ft, about 2 1/2 hours, landing at night at an unfamiliar airport.

steps.s: At 2200 the operator confirms the 0600 departure. You finished one glass of wine at 2100. What do you do?
options: Fly at 0600; it is more than 8 hours
Fly at 0600 after strong coffee to clear the alcohol
Fly at 0600 but stay below 10,000 ft
Ask to move departure to 0900 or later, at least 12 hours after the drink
steps.why: 0600 is legal under 91.17 [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]], but the AIM's rule is at least 12 to 24 hours, and nothing speeds up the destruction of alcohol [[34:181|AIM 8-1-1]].

steps.s: At the airplane, one passenger is slurring and unsteady after an all-night party. He is not a patient and there is no emergency.
options: Carry him; he is a paying customer
Carry him if the other passenger agrees
Do not carry him
Carry him if he sits in the back
steps.why: Except in an emergency, no pilot may allow a person who appears intoxicated to be carried, unless a medical patient under proper care [[60:437|14 CFR 91.17]].

steps.s: You have been level at 11,500 ft for 35 minutes without oxygen. You feel great but have a mild headache.
options: Continue; 91.211 does not apply below 12,500 ft
Put on oxygen now, or descend below 10,000 ft
Climb above 12,000 ft to get on top of the haze
Breathe faster to get more oxygen
steps.why: Part 135 requires oxygen above 10,000 ft through 12,000 ft for the part over 30 minutes [[6:26|14 CFR 135.89]]. Euphoria and headache are hypoxia symptoms [[1:426|PHAK 17-4]], and breathing faster invites hyperventilation [[34:184|AIM 8-1-3]].

steps.s: Later, with the cabin heater on, a passenger complains of a headache and drowsiness. You notice a faint exhaust smell.
options: Heater off, fresh air vents and windows open, oxygen on, land and seek medical care if symptoms persist
Turn the heater up so everyone stays warm
Ignore it; CO always has a strong smell
Open the vents but keep the heater on
steps.why: Suspect CO: shut off the heater, open fresh air vents and windows, use supplemental oxygen, and get treatment if symptoms are severe or continue after landing [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]] [[34:184|AIM 8-1-4]].

steps.s: At night you approach the unfamiliar airport over dark, featureless terrain. The runway slopes up and you feel high. A PAPI is working.
options: Reduce power and descend to fix the high picture
Level off until the runway looks normal
Steepen the approach to land short
Fly the PAPI and cross-check the altimeter
steps.why: Featureless terrain and an upsloping runway create the illusion of being higher than you are, leading to a low approach [[34:186|AIM 8-1-5]]. Use the PAPI and the altimeter [[1:433|PHAK 17-11]].
